column5: gain the world, forfeit the life
column6: The commentary makes the trader's final capital his own self; Jesus asks what profit the whole world brings if a person forfeits his life, making the apparent gain a net personal loss.

column5: gain world, lose self
column6: The commentary reads loss of one's self as the last entry in the account; this verse explicitly asks what benefit remains when a person gains the world but loses or forfeits himself.

column5: former gains counted loss
column6: The commentary distinguishes apparent accumulation from the true balance; Paul says things once counted as gains became loss for Christ, reversing his own ledger.

column5: all things loss, Christ gain
column6: The commentary's trade between perishing capital and lasting gain has a close counterpart in Paul's reckoning of everything as loss compared with gaining Christ.

column5: profit from toil under the sun
column6: The commentary joins time, work and the merchant's question about real gain; Ecclesiastes asks what profit a human has from all the toil he toils under the sun.

column5: root table ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary puts a lifetime's work in the loss account; the speaker surveys works done by his hands and the עמל spent on them, finding no lasting profit under the sun.

column5: counting days for wisdom
column6: The commentary treats passing time as spent capital; the psalm asks God to teach humans to number their days so that they gain a wise heart.

column5: brief years filled with toil
column6: The commentary's late day and dwindling lifetime meet this psalm's seventy or eighty years, their toil and trouble, and their swift passing.

column5: riches fail on day of wrath
column6: The commentary contrasts counted money with the final moral account; the proverb says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death.

column5: ill-gotten treasure versus righteousness
column6: The commentary's profitable trade through right action meets the proverb's claim that wicked treasure yields no profit but righteousness rescues from death.

column5: stored wealth, life required tonight
column6: The commentary sets money counted as increase against the loss of the owner himself; God asks the rich fool whose stored goods will be his when his life is demanded that night.

column5: self-stored treasure versus true wealth
column6: The commentary describes a hidden deficit while possessions grow; Jesus concludes that one who stores treasure for himself can fail to be rich toward God.

column5: imagined wealth, unrecognized poverty
column6: The commentary stresses a loss one does not feel; Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing while failing to know its poverty and blindness.

column5: Moses notices fire in the wilderness
column6: The commentary follows Moses noticing fire on a journey and seeking guidance; Exodus places the divine fire in a bush that burns without being consumed, specifying the sight he is drawn to investigate.

column5: Moses turns to inspect unconsumed bush
column6: In the commentary's Qur'anic scene Moses hopes for an ember or guide for his family; in Exodus he turns aside to inspect why the burning bush is not consumed, a different immediate purpose for approaching the fire.

column5: unjust measures and weights prohibited
column6: The commentary's seller secretly reduces the buyer's portion; Leviticus forbids injustice in measures of length, weight and quantity, grounding the market image in a concrete legal rule.

column5: two different weights in one bag
column6: The commentary describes one trader using different scales depending on whether he takes or gives; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small weight together in one's bag.

column5: small measure, great price, false balances
column6: The commentary's two-directional fraud matches merchants in Amos who shrink the ephah, enlarge the shekel and falsify balances while selling grain.

column5: false balance versus just weight
column6: The commentary joins fair weighing to moral truth; the proverb calls a false balance abominable to the Lord and a just weight his delight.

column5: God weighs the person on a just balance
column6: The commentary moves from market scales to the weighing of a person's own worth; Job asks that God weigh him in a just balance and know his integrity.

column5: root table خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary joins a deficient balance to personal loss; Daniel interprets TEKEL as the king weighed in the balances and found חַסִּיר, lacking.

column5: king weighed and found wanting
column6: The commentary's final scale finds the person himself light rather than a short measure of goods; Daniel pronounces that the king has been weighed and found deficient.

column5: way seeming right ends in death
column6: The commentary's gravest loser believes his work is good while straying; this proverb says a way can seem right to a person yet end in the ways of death.

column5: all people straying like sheep
column6: The commentary says its judgment first includes the whole human kind and describes loss as going astray; Isaiah says all like sheep have strayed, each turning to his own way.

column5: all turned aside, none doing good
column6: The commentary's generic human is under a negative verdict before an exception is named; the psalm says all have turned aside and none does good, giving a parallel universal diagnosis.

column5: all sin and fall short
column6: The commentary emphasizes a judgment on humanity as a class; Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, a comparably universal shortfall.

column5: created upright, sought schemes
column6: The commentary contrasts the human's good created condition with a later loss; Ecclesiastes says God made humanity upright but people sought many schemes.

column5: return to dust after mortal labor
column6: The commentary treats time and the self as capital that finally runs out; the judgment on Adam makes his eating by sweat end in a return to dust.

column5: work tested by fire on the day
column6: The commentary joins work, judgment and a fire storm that can erase a lifetime's produce; Paul says the Day and its fire disclose the quality of each person's work.

column5: work lost while person saved
column6: The commentary's ultimate deficit can be loss of the self; Paul describes a person's work burning and that person suffering loss yet being saved through fire, a narrower outcome for loss.

column5: fruit dried by east wind and burned
column6: The commentary imagines a life's crop ruined by a destructive wind with fire; Ezekiel's vine is uprooted, its fruit dried by the east wind and its branches consumed by fire.

column5: storm destroys house without secure foundation
column6: The commentary opposes a refuge to exposure when destructive weather arrives; Jesus' rain, floods and winds strike the house built on sand, which falls greatly.

column5: face reflected in water, heart answered by another
column6: The commentary's small image of a person seen in another's eye bridges solitary self-knowledge and mutual counsel; the proverb makes a reflected face the analogy for one human heart answering another.

column5: reprove neighbor to prevent shared sin
column6: The commentary's escape from loss includes people recommending truth to one another; Leviticus requires frank correction of a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin because of him.

column5: exhort one another every day called Today
column6: The commentary unites expiring time with reciprocal advice against unnoticed ruin; Hebrews tells believers to exhort one another each day lest sin's deceit harden anyone.

column5: mutual stirring toward love and good deeds
column6: The commentary's exception joins good action to mutual counsel; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to stir love and good works.

column5: mortal returned to dust
column6: The commentary's generic human remains in an ongoing condition of loss; this psalm addresses God as returning mortals to dust, putting humanity inside a bounded mortal state.

column5: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
column6: The commentary names the generic visible human and asks what loss takes from such a being; the psalm calls the person אֱנוֹשׁ while asking why God remembers him, emphasizing mortal smallness beside divine regard.

column5: root table ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary links truth, the appointed day and a life's spent time; Job says a human's days and months are fixed and God has set his limits, using a form of חק for the allotted boundary.

column5: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary calls loss an unmeasured deficit in an account; Ecclesiastes says what is lacking, חֶסְרוֹן, cannot be counted, joining deficiency with reckoning while leaving the shortfall unresolved.

column5: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's alternative to losing one's capital is right use of it; this proverb says the one who gives to the poor will not lack, using חסר for lack and making generosity the decisive transaction.

column5: appointed time to judge every work
column6: The commentary relates the passing hour to a day that brings each deed to account; Ecclesiastes says God will judge righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.

column5: lack of sense and self-destruction
column6: The commentary joins failing perception with losing oneself; Proverbs says the adulterer lacks sense and destroys his own life, making a hidden deficit in judgment lead to self-loss.

column5: claim to see leaves sin remaining
column6: The commentary's seeing human may fail to perceive his own loss; Jesus tells his hearers that because they say they see, their sin remains.

column5: entrusted money traded to gain more
column6: The commentary reads the lifetime as trading capital placed in human hands; the first servant immediately trades his master's five talents and gains five more.

column5: talent buried in fear
column6: The commentary distinguishes merely retaining possessions from making a profitable moral return; the fearful servant hides the entrusted talent in the ground and returns only the original sum.

column5: unused capital taken away
column6: The commentary says loss can consume the principal itself; Jesus' conclusion to the talents story says the one who has not will lose even what he has.

column5: short day, much work, great wage
column6: The commentary imagines time as the trader's expiring capital and good deeds as work for gain; R. Tarfon's saying turns the short day, plentiful work and great wage into an urgent moral account.

column5: labor incomplete, employer pays wage
column6: The commentary's exceptions are counted by belief and deeds rather than by ancestry; Avot says one need not finish the work yet may not cease from it, and a faithful employer pays the wage.

column5: open shop, ledger, collectors and true judgment
column6: The commentary's market account and final balance meet Avot's shop on credit, open ledger recording actions, daily collectors and judgment declared true.

column5: this world as antechamber, preparation beyond
column6: The commentary places the human inside a temporal condition whose use determines later gain; Avot calls this world an antechamber and urges preparation there before entering the banquet hall.

column5: faith without works is dead
column6: The commentary notes that the exception from human loss names faith together with good works; James makes the link pointed by declaring faith dead when it has no works.

column5: good work and future harvest
column6: The commentary puts right action against an otherwise diminishing life's work; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in due season if one does not give up.

column5: wealth flies away when gazed at
column6: The commentary's rich counter can grow while true capital melts away; Proverbs asks whether one fixes eyes on wealth that vanishes and flies toward heaven.

column5: toiler departs with nothing in hand
column6: The commentary's trader can spend the principal of life and end empty; Ecclesiastes says a person departs naked as he came and takes nothing from his toil in his hand.

column5: great wealth destroyed in one hour
column6: The commentary connects the late hour to a lifetime's accumulated goods lost suddenly; the lament over Babylon says its great wealth has been laid waste in one hour.

column5: gain whole world, forfeit life
column6: The commentary says worldly profit can conceal loss of the person; Mark's version of Jesus' question uses the same economic comparison between gaining the world and forfeiting life.

column5: all appear for recompense of deeds
column6: The commentary's universal human category and final scale lead to deeds being reckoned; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they have done in the body.

column5: death once, then judgment
column6: The commentary spends the mortal's time toward an appointed day of reckoning; Hebrews places judgment after each human's one death.

column5: nothing brought in or taken out
column6: The commentary contrasts counted goods with the person's last balance; Paul says people brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out.

column5: faithful management of small trust
column6: The commentary uses the orphan's property to connect discerned maturity with entrusted capital; Jesus says reliability in a small matter shows reliability in a great one.

column5: trustworthiness with wealth tested
column6: The commentary's guardian sees whether a ward is ready to receive property; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with unrighteous wealth.

column5: minor heir under guardians until set time
column6: The commentary cites testing an orphan's maturity before releasing property; Paul describes an heir who, while a child, remains under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time.

column5: warning not to afflict widow or orphan
column6: The commentary treats an orphan's property as a trust needing care; Exodus forbids afflicting the vulnerable widow or orphan, supplying the ethical duty behind such guardianship.

column5: whole creation pronounced very good
column6: The commentary contrasts humanity's given good beginning with its later place inside loss; Genesis records God's judgment that all he made was very good.

column5: death spread to all people
column6: The commentary places the human kind, not one individual, under an enveloping negative condition; Paul says death passed to all people after sin entered the world.

column5: justification offered after universal shortfall
column6: The commentary names an exception after its universal verdict; immediately after Paul's statement that all fall short, he says people are justified by grace through Christ, an alternate account of escape.

column5: salvation not from works
column6: The commentary's exception explicitly joins faith with righteous deeds; Paul denies that salvation comes from works, sharpening a difference in how the saving relation of deeds is stated.

column5: way of wicked perishes
column6: The commentary extends loss to losing one's way and finally perishing; the psalm contrasts God's knowledge of the righteous way with the way of the wicked that perishes.

column5: broad way leading to destruction
column6: The commentary's traveler eats through provisions after losing direction and faces ruin; Jesus describes a spacious road on which many travel toward destruction.

column5: lost son comes to himself
column6: The commentary calls the last loss a loss of oneself and also stresses failure to perceive it; the son in the parable comes to himself after dissipating his property and falling into hunger.

column5: dead, alive; lost, found
column6: The commentary juxtaposes loss of property, self and companionship; the father describes the returning son as lost and found and celebrates restored family relation.

column5: apparently right road ends in death
column6: The commentary says the worst loss is the laborer who thinks his route sound; a second proverb states that a seemingly right human way ends in death.

column5: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
column6: The commentary says the human who can notice things may miss his own deficit; Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful and אנש, desperately sick, then asks who can know it.

column5: God searches heart and repays deeds
column6: The commentary opposes self-deception to an objective account of actions; Jeremiah's next verse says the Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to his ways and deeds.

column5: minds blinded against seeing light
column6: The commentary's named seeing being fails to see the situation he is in; Paul says the minds of unbelievers are blinded so they do not see the gospel's light.

column5: clear self-sight before helping brother
column6: The commentary's reflected self in another's eye leads to reciprocal truth telling; Jesus says first to remove one's own obstruction so one can see clearly to help a brother with his.

column5: indirect reflection and eventual face-to-face sight
column6: The commentary uses a tiny reflected face to describe limited self-knowledge through another person; Paul describes present seeing through a mirror dimly and later face-to-face knowing.

column5: friend sharpens friend like iron
column6: The commentary says the solitary human emerges from loss through others' counsel; Proverbs makes one person sharpen another as iron sharpens iron.

column5: acquire a friend and teacher
column6: The commentary moves from the isolated human to someone who receives truth from another; Avot tells a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, naming relationships as part of moral formation.

column5: do not separate from community
column6: The commentary treats companionship and mutual counsel as an exit from solitary loss; this maxim explicitly warns against separating oneself from the community.

column5: encourage and build one another
column6: The commentary's third verse replaces the isolated figure with mutual exhortation; Paul directs believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

column5: bear one another's burdens
column6: The commentary develops a beast carrying a load and then humans helping each other on the way; Paul converts burden bearing into a reciprocal command among people.

column5: root table ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary hears refuge against destruction in the first verse's secondary sense; the plague is עָצַר, stopped, after Phinehas intervenes, offering a concrete image of destruction held back rather than a claim that the Arabic and Hebrew senses are identical.

column5: wealth heaped like dust
column6: The commentary exposes the illusion that ever more counted wealth is safety; Job pictures the wicked heaping silver like dust before describing how another will wear it. Hebrew צבר in the root table is only a sound correspondence to Arabic صبر, not evidence of a shared meaning here.

column5: use wealth to make friends and find dwelling
column6: The commentary makes reciprocal companionship an alternative to loss in the market; Jesus urges using temporary wealth to make friends who will welcome one into lasting dwellings.

column5: remember origin, end and final accounting
column6: The commentary's human has an unseen deficit that an appointed day reveals; Avot asks a person to remember his beginning, his end and before whom he must give account.

column5: life and death lead to an account
column6: The commentary speaks of each human brought to his due day with his deeds; Avot insists that birth, life, death and the eventual account before the divine king are inescapable.

column5: hearing and doing make a secure house
column6: The commentary's refuge against a ruinous storm depends on faith and good action; Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a house built on rock.

column5: wealth gained quickly dwindles
column6: The commentary's business account distinguishes growing sums from preserving principal; the proverb says wealth gained hastily diminishes while gathered wealth grows steadily.

column5: withheld wages cry against owner
column6: The commentary's dishonest measure makes another person's principal short; James says wages withheld from harvest laborers cry out, turning economic theft into a charge before God.

column5: honest complete weight lengthens days
column6: The commentary joins accurate scales to one's own final condition; Deuteronomy commands a full and just weight so that the people's days may be long in the land.

column5: what one sows, one reaps
column6: The commentary's lost cultivated produce connects present deeds to a later account; Paul says people reap what they sow, making the harvest an ethical measure.

column5: root table ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's generic insan is initially lost but its exception allows another outcome; Daniel sees one like a son of אֱנָשׁ brought before the Ancient of Days, an exalted humanlike figure. The link is limited because Daniel presents a vision figure, not a verdict on humanity as a whole.

column5: gathered water and storm clouds
column6: The commentary imagines loss outside a shelter under destructive weather; David's rescue song pictures God surrounded by gathered water and thick clouds. The root table's Hebrew חשר has a possible sound relation to Arabic خ س ر but the cloud word does not mean loss; this is only an atmospheric image meeting.

column5: companionship or death in Honi's return
column6: The commentary says the human needs others to escape solitary loss; the Honi story ends with his isolation when others do not recognize him and the maxim that one needs companionship or death. This extends the commentary's social image rather than interpreting its verse directly.
